definition: A signaling chemical stored in platelet dense granules; at a wound it helps keep the vessel narrowed.
A fat that is part of cell membranes. Enzymes like COX-1 turn it into signaling molecules such as thromboxane A2.
Storage packets inside the cells lining blood vessels; they hold von Willebrand factor until it is needed.
A liver enzyme that processes many drugs. It converts clopidogrel into its active form; some people's version works poorly.
The dragging force of blood flowing past a surface; it is strongest in fast-flowing arteries.
A rare inherited platelet disorder in which platelets lack working GPIb, so they cannot stick properly to von Willebrand factor.
A rare inherited platelet disorder in which platelets lack GPIIb/IIIa, so they cannot clump together.
The medical word for a nosebleed.
Narrowing of a blood vessel when the muscle in its wall tightens.
Widening of a blood vessel when the muscle in its wall relaxes.
The main fat molecule that makes up cell membranes. On activated platelets, some of it faces outward and gives clotting factors a place to gather.
An inherited bleeding disorder caused by too little factor VIII; bleeding tends to go deep, into joints and muscles.
A second ADP receptor on platelets, alongside P2Y12. The antiplatelet drugs in this module block P2Y12, not P2Y1.
Taking aspirin plus a P2Y12 blocker (such as clopidogrel) together, often after a heart attack or a coronary stent.
The time it takes for the amount of a drug in the blood to drop by half. For irreversible antiplatelet drugs, the effect lasts much longer than the drug's half-life.
Signals from inside an activated platelet that switch its GPIIb/IIIa receptor into the shape that can grab fibrinogen.
A lab reagent that makes von Willebrand factor bind platelets; used in tests for von Willebrand disease.
An older test that measures how long a small standard cut takes to stop bleeding; it reflects platelet function.
